title: Bob Dylan Comes Knockin' on the Pope's Door
summary: Bob Dylan came knockin' on the pope's door on Wednesday. The American singer-songwriter visited Pope Leo XIV, the American pope, at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy. The Vatican said the meeting was brief. Leo gave Dylan a rosary, and Dylan gave the pope a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One." The two men had a connection before they ever met. Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan wrote in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift." In the book, Leo warned against the race to rearm and the use of nuclear weapons, quoting the song's words to a make-believe atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled." Dylan was accompanied by two Vatican officials, the Rev. Antonio Spadaro and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper. Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. Spadaro also noted that Dylan knows the work of St. Augustine of Hippo well, and Dylan wrote "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine" for his 1967 album "John Wesley Harding." Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie for the meeting, with the hood over his head in the Vatican photos. This was not his first meeting with a pope: he played for Pope John Paul II in 1997 at a concert in Bologna, Italy. Dylan, who was born Robert Zimmerman, told the Wall Street Journal in 2022 that he was a "religious person" who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays. At his most recent concert before the Vatican visit, he sang his 1997 song "Tryin' to Get to Heaven."
why_it_matters: Music and faith both bring people together, and a meeting between a famous singer and the pope shows how the two can connect.
